imp.voice_memo:
Chandler writes like a man who finds the world faintly ridiculous and entirely dangerous, and can't decide which bothers him more. The voice is Marlowe's — first person, past tense, moving through a fallen city with his collar up and his irony loaded. The rhythm is the thing to get right first: short declarative sentences that hit like a fist, then a long sinuous one that coils around a metaphor and squeezes. He'll drop a plain fact — 'It was a Tuesday' — then immediately corrupt it with a simile that's funny and bleak at once, the way Tuesdays 'go bad faster than milk in August.' That pivot, from the flat to the lyrical, is his signature move.

He reaches for similes the way other writers reach for adjectives, and they're never decorative — they carry moral weight. 'A smile like a cracked sidewalk.' A voice that 'carried just enough trouble in it to fill a hearse.' The comparisons are always slightly wrong in a way that's exactly right, yoking beauty to damage, elegance to rot. He refuses abstraction almost entirely; every emotion gets rendered as a physical object or a weather system.

His sentences love to double back on themselves — 'the way it had said nothing for three days, the way a dead man says nothing when you ask him who pulled the trigger' — building a quiet, sardonic music through repetition. He's funny, but the jokes are load-bearing; they keep the despair from becoming melodrama. The city is always present as atmosphere, always wet or neon-smeared or smelling of something surrendered. And underneath all of it runs a current of exhausted decency — a man who knows the price of everything and keeps paying it anyway.
